The Psychology Behind Designing Digital Products People Can Use

This page is not just a lecture summary. It is a reusable toolkit to help you think more clearly when you design a product, service, feature, workflow, or AI interaction.

See the examples Use the framework Open the resources
The one habit to keep

Stop asking only, “Does this make sense to me?” Start asking, “How will someone else understand this?”

Why psychology matters

Every interface quietly makes assumptions about attention, memory, emotion, trust, motivation, and effort.

What this helps you do

Spot hidden friction, understand behaviour, and design with more empathy and fewer wrong guesses.

How to use this page

Read top to bottom, or jump to the section you need when you are working on an assignment or prototype.

How a user experiences a product

The design-to-behaviour loop

A screen is only the middle of the experience. People arrive with expectations, interpret what they see, act, read the response, and carry that learning into the next interaction.

Use this to diagnose a screen, flow, or feature

Follow what happens before, during, and after the tap.

Psychology sits across the whole loop
The interface is not the whole experience.

Psychology helps you understand what happens before a tap, during a decision, and after the system responds.

The five lenses

Five ways to inspect any digital product.

These are not rigid theories to memorize. They are practical lenses you can use when you are evaluating screens, features, flows, and user behaviour.

👀

Attention

People do not see everything. They notice what stands out and ignore what competes too hard.

Ask: What can users notice first, and what might they miss?
🧠

Expectation

People bring assumptions from past products, habits, and norms.

Ask: What do users think will happen when they tap this?
⚡

Effort

Every tap, choice, re-entry, and delay costs something.

Ask: Is the task harder than it needs to be?
🔁

Feedback

Users need to know what just happened, what is happening now, and what to do next.

Ask: Does the system clearly show status and consequences?
🎯

Motivation

What you reward, people do more of. What you punish, they avoid.

Ask: What behaviour is the design encouraging?
Real examples

Examples are where the psychology becomes visible.

Each example pairs a problem with a more useful approach. The goal is not to judge the product. The goal is to train your eye.

Case 1. Friction

Sometimes a product makes leaving harder than joining. Sometimes a product removes steps so people can get a task done with less effort. That difference is a design decision.

Problem

Amazon Prime cancellation

The issue was not just that there was a cancellation option. The problem was the amount of friction wrapped around the exit flow.

Account→Menu→More steps→Confirm
Better approach

Myinfo and Toss

Both are useful reminders that a system can reduce re-entry and unnecessary repetition for tasks users already want to complete.

Known info→Confirm→Done
Design takeaway: Every extra step is a cost. Ask who is paying it, and why.

Case 2. Context

Users do not interact with products in ideal conditions. They use them in places, routines, time pressure, distractions, and physical environments.

Problem

MyPertamina

When an app becomes part of a fuel-purchase flow, the user is not just thinking about the screen. They are also dealing with phone access, signal, battery, and safety around the pump.

phonesignalbatterysafe use
Better approach

Google Maps motorcycle mode

This is a context-aware design response. The product studied actual riders, local routes, and the needs of a specific mode of transport.

real riders→local streets→useful guidance
Design takeaway: Design for the place and situation where the task actually happens.

Case 3. Expectations

A familiar product creates habits. Once those habits exist, major changes create a relearning cost. That cost is psychological, not just technical.

Problem

Redesign backlash

Products such as Instagram and Sonos remind us that even a cleaner-looking redesign can fail if it breaks what users already know how to do.

learned habit→major change→relearning cost
Better approach

QRIS

QRIS is a strong example of a standard that protects familiarity. Different providers can still preserve one clear mental model.

scan→confirm→pay
Design takeaway: A habit is part of the interface. Change it carefully.

Case 4. Feedback

Users act on what the system shows them. If the status is unclear, the confirmation is weak, or recovery is slow, people can make serious mistakes.

Problem

Hawaii false missile alert

The key lesson is not just “an error happened.” The deeper lesson is that interfaces need strong separation between test and live actions, clear confirmation, and fast recovery.

Illustrative alert state
Emergency alert
If a test action and a live action are too easy to confuse, users will trust the wrong signal.
testliveweak confirmationslow correction
Better approach

Figma multiplayer

This is a useful contrast because it makes activity visible. You can see what others are doing, where they are working, and what is changing in real time.

User A editing
User B reviewing
Illustrative mock. The point is visible status, visible collaboration, and easier shared understanding.
action→visible status→shared understanding
Design takeaway: Show status, consequence, and recovery clearly.

Case 5. Motivation

Design does not just make action possible. It can also shape what people want to do next, how often they do it, and whether the behaviour helps or harms them.

Problem

Robinhood and reward-heavy design

When the interface makes a serious activity feel exciting, frictionless, and celebratory, it can push behaviour beyond what is healthy for the user.

Engagement signalFast, exciting, easy to repeat
User-benefit questionDoes it improve the quality of the decision?
reward→behaviour→real-world consequence
Better approach

Duolingo streaks

Gamification is not automatically bad. It depends on what behaviour it strengthens and whether it supports a meaningful user goal.

routine→streak→flexibility
Design takeaway: Measure whether the behaviour helps the user, not only whether it keeps them active.
Core framework

A simple workflow you can reuse.

This can guide your assignments, design reviews, and prototype critiques. It is intentionally simple so you can remember it under pressure.

1Understand the task
2Identify the assumptions
3Design the flow
4Test with someone
5Improve it
Remember this

Good design is translation.

It translates what the builder intends into something the user can understand quickly, correctly, and with low effort.

Builder

Has goals, features, KPIs, constraints.

Interface

Turns intent into screens, words, and interactions.

User

Sees only what the product communicates in the moment.

Someone-Else Check

A checklist you can use before and after building.

If you remember only one applied habit from this toolkit, let it be this: always test whether another person understands your design the way you think they will.

Before

Before you build

  • ◎What is the user actually trying to achieve?
  • ↳What does the user already know before they arrive?
  • ?Which part of the task is most likely to confuse them?
  • −What information is essential, and what can be removed?
  • ✓What does success look like from the user’s point of view?
After

After you build

  • ▶Can someone complete the task without your help?
  • ⌁Where do they hesitate, guess, or go back?
  • ≠What do they expect that the product does not provide?
  • ↺Can they explain the flow back in their own words?
  • ✦What one change would reduce confusion the most?
Builder
prototypeobserverevise
Someone else

The check works because it creates distance between what you meant and what another person can actually infer.

Practice tools

Train your eye, not just your vocabulary.

The fastest way to improve is to analyse real screens repeatedly. Use the exercises below as short design workouts.

01

Attention scan

Look at a screen for five seconds, then hide it. Write down what you remember. What dominated attention and what disappeared?

First focal pointCompeting elementsMissed information
02

Flow teardown

Choose one task such as sign up, checkout, booking, or cancelling. Map every step, decision, wait, and recovery point.

Count decisionsFind frictionMark recovery
Start
→
Choose
→
Wait?
→
Confirm
What if something fails?
03

Behaviour loop

Identify the trigger, action, reward, and consequence. Then ask whether the loop helps the user reach a meaningful goal.

TriggerActionRewardConsequence
User goalTriggerActionRewardResult
Practice on real screens

Pick one screen and ask three questions.

Why was it designed this way? What else could the designer have chosen? Who would each version work better for?

Q and A starters

Questions worth asking in class or in critique.

When does helpful persuasion become manipulation?
Should a beautiful interface ever be allowed to make a task harder?
If AI can build an interface fast, what becomes more important for the human designer?
How much user feedback is enough before building?
Can a product succeed for the company but still be bad for the user?
Which matters more here: reducing steps, or reducing uncertainty?

Final reminder

Good design reduces the distance between what the builder intends and what the user understands.

Use this page as a toolkit, not just as reading material. Revisit the five lenses, compare the examples, and run the Someone-Else Check whenever you build something new.
